source.title: Eat That Frog!
source.attribution: Summary in our own words of Eat That Frog! by Brian Tracy (2001). Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.
source.notes: Original summary written by Reborn; contains no text from the book. The book is in copyright.

cards.title: Do your hardest, most important task first
cards.body:
Tracy's central image is the "frog": the big, unpleasant task you are most likely to put off, yet the one that would make the biggest difference if done. His advice is to tackle it first, before easier work fills the day.

Getting it done early removes the background dread, and the momentum carries into everything else. If you have two frogs, start with the uglier one. Clearing email or small chores first feels productive, but it usually just delays the work that actually matters.
cards.apply_it: Tonight, choose tomorrow's frog: the one task that matters most. Start it first thing, before checking messages.

quiz.question: In Tracy's metaphor, what is your 'frog'?
options: Your most important task, often the one you're avoiding
quiz.explanation: The frog is the important, unpleasant task you are most tempted to put off.

cards.title: Plan your day on paper before it starts
cards.body:
Tracy insists that working from a written list, made in advance, is one of the simplest ways to get more done. Ideally you draw it up the evening before, so you start the day knowing what to do.

He argues that a few minutes of planning saves far more time in execution, because you stop bouncing between tasks and deciding what to do next. Writing things down also clears your head. Add new tasks to the list as they come up rather than reacting to them straight away.
cards.apply_it: Before you finish work today, write tomorrow's task list and put your single most important task at the top.

quiz.question: When does Tracy suggest making your daily task list?
options: In the middle of the day
Never; keep it in your head
quiz.explanation: Planning in advance means you begin the day already knowing what to tackle.

cards.title: A few of your tasks produce most of your results
cards.body:
Tracy applies the 80/20 principle to work: a small share of your activities tends to account for most of the value you create. On a list of ten tasks, one or two may be worth more than all the rest combined.

The trap is that people busy themselves with the many low-value items because they are quick and easy. Before starting, ask which items on your list will really move things forward, and put your best time and energy there.
cards.apply_it: Look at your current to-do list and circle the one or two items that would create the most value. Do those first.

quiz.question: What does the 80/20 rule suggest about your task list?
options: A small number of tasks deliver most of the value
You should do the quickest tasks first
quiz.explanation: A minority of activities typically drives the majority of results.

cards.title: Rank tasks by consequence, from must-do to cut entirely
cards.body:
Tracy suggests grading every item on your list by what happens if you do or don't do it. Tasks with serious consequences come first; things that would be nice but matter little come later; some can be handed to someone else; and some can simply be dropped.

This "ABCDE" style of ranking forces honest choices. You only move to a lower-grade task when the higher ones are done. Thinking about consequences, including long-term ones, is what separates real priorities from busywork.
cards.apply_it: Label each task on today's list with A to E by consequence. Delegate the Ds, delete the Es, and start with your top A.

quiz.question: In Tracy's ranking method, what decides a task's priority?
options: Who asked for it most recently
The consequences of doing or not doing it
quiz.explanation: Tasks with the biggest consequences come first; low-consequence ones are delegated or dropped.

cards.title: Choose deliberately what you will not do
cards.body:
Everyone procrastinates on something, Tracy notes, because there is always more to do than time allows. The question is whether you put off the right things.

He calls this creative procrastination: consciously deciding to delay or abandon low-value tasks so you have time for high-value ones. That might mean saying no to requests, dropping a habitual activity, or leaving minor tasks undone. Starting something new means stopping something else, so make those trade-offs on purpose rather than by default.
cards.apply_it: List three low-value activities that take up your time each week. Choose one to stop or postpone indefinitely.

quiz.question: What does Tracy mean by 'creative procrastination'?
options: Deliberately putting off low-value tasks to make room for important ones
Delaying hard tasks until the deadline
Doing creative hobbies instead of work
quiz.explanation: Since you can't do everything, you consciously postpone the things that matter least.

cards.title: Once you start an important task, stay with it until it's done
cards.body:
Tracy argues that starting and stopping a task repeatedly wastes huge amounts of time, because each restart means getting back up to speed. His advice is to single-handle it: once you begin, keep going without switching until it is finished.

Sustained focus also builds momentum and the satisfaction of completion, which makes the next big task easier to start. In a world of notifications and open tabs, this means deliberately protecting a block of time with distractions switched off.
cards.apply_it: Block 60-90 minutes for your most important task. Turn off notifications and don't switch tasks until it's done or the block ends.

quiz.question: Why does Tracy advise staying with one task until it's complete?
options: Because switching back and forth wastes time getting back up to speed
quiz.explanation: Each restart costs time and focus; finishing in one go is far more efficient.

cards.title: Get clear on your goals and write them down
cards.body:
Tracy argues that a lack of clarity is one of the biggest causes of procrastination: when you aren't sure what you're trying to achieve, it's easy to drift. He offers a simple sequence: decide exactly what you want, write it down, set a deadline, list everything you'd need to do, organise that list into a plan, take some action right away, and do something towards the goal every day.

Writing turns a vague wish into something concrete you can act on and check against. A clear target also makes it easier to spot your frog each day.
cards.apply_it: Write one goal on paper with a deadline, then list three steps toward it. Do the first step today.

quiz.question: Why does Tracy put so much weight on clear, written goals?
options: Unclear goals make it easy to drift and procrastinate
quiz.explanation: Clarity about what you want makes it easier to act and to pick the right tasks.

cards.title: Let your long-term future guide today's choices
cards.body:
Tracy cites the Harvard sociologist Edward Banfield, who concluded that a long time perspective was a strong predictor of people's upward economic mobility. People who think about where they want to be in five or ten years tend to make better decisions about what to do today.

Tracy applies this to tasks: before choosing what to work on, think about the likely consequences over time. Something that matters for your future deserves priority over something that only feels urgent now. Sacrificing short-term comfort for long-term gain is a habit successful people tend to share.
cards.apply_it: Before starting your next task, ask: what difference will this make a year from now? Let the answer set your order.

quiz.question: What does Tracy draw from Banfield's research?
options: Thinking long term leads to better choices about what to do now
Short-term pleasure is the key to success
Planning is a waste of time
quiz.explanation: A long time perspective helps you choose tasks with lasting consequences.

cards.title: You'll never have time for everything, but you can do what matters most
cards.body:
Tracy calls this the law of forced efficiency: there is never enough time to do everything, but there is always enough time to do the most important thing. When pressure rises, you are forced to choose.

The lesson is to stop trying to clear every item and instead make sure the critical ones get done. He also cautions against relying on last-minute rushes; work done in a panic tends to bring more stress and mistakes. Choose the important thing early and give it your best hours.
cards.apply_it: Accept that some things won't get done today. Write the single thing that must get done, and protect time for it.

quiz.question: What does Tracy's law of forced efficiency state?
options: You can always finish everything with enough effort
There's never time for everything, but always time for the most important thing
quiz.explanation: Time is limited, so the priority is to make sure the most important task is done.

cards.title: Keep asking: what is the most valuable use of my time right now?
cards.body:
Tracy offers a few questions to keep you on track through the day. What are my highest-value activities? What can I, and only I, do that would make a real difference if done well? And, above all, what is the most valuable use of my time right now?

These questions cut through the noise of emails, requests and easy tasks. Asking them regularly helps you notice when you've drifted into busywork and steer back to the work that counts. The answer to the last question is usually your frog.
cards.apply_it: Write 'What is the most valuable use of my time right now?' on a note by your desk. Ask it every time you switch tasks.

quiz.question: Which question does Tracy treat as central to managing your time?
options: What's the quickest task I can finish?
What is the most valuable use of my time right now?
What do other people want me to do?
How can I avoid hard work today?
quiz.explanation: Asking it repeatedly keeps attention on the highest-value task.

cards.title: Ask whether you would start this today, knowing what you know now
cards.body:
Tracy suggests zero-based thinking: regularly look at your commitments, projects and activities and ask, 'If I weren't already doing this, would I start it today, knowing what I now know?'

If the answer is no, the next question is how quickly you can get out of it. Many people keep going with things only because they started them, wasting time and energy on work that no longer makes sense. This simple test frees up room for your priorities.
cards.apply_it: Apply the question to one ongoing commitment this week. If the answer is no, plan how to wind it down.

quiz.question: What question lies at the heart of zero-based thinking?
options: How can I do this faster?
Would I start this today, knowing what I know now?
quiz.explanation: If you wouldn't start it again now, it may be time to stop doing it.

cards.title: Know the few results your job really exists to deliver
cards.body:
Tracy suggests that every job can be broken into a handful of key result areas, usually five to seven: the results you are fully responsible for and that you are paid to deliver. A salesperson's might include finding prospects, presenting and closing.

Identifying them clarifies what deserves your time. Ask yourself why you are on the payroll, and check whether your days are spent on those core results or on activities that feel busy but don't move them. If you're unsure, discuss it with your manager or clients.
cards.apply_it: List the five to seven results you are most responsible for at work. Compare it with how you spent yesterday.

quiz.question: What are 'key result areas' in Tracy's book?
options: The core results you're responsible for and paid to deliver
quiz.explanation: They are the essential outputs your role exists to produce.

cards.title: Your weakest key skill sets the ceiling for your overall results
cards.body:
Tracy argues that weakness in any one of your key result areas can hold back your overall performance, much like a weak link in a chain. A great salesperson who can't follow up, or a skilled manager who can't delegate, is limited by that gap.

He suggests rating yourself honestly from 1 to 10 in each key area, then identifying the one where improvement would make the biggest difference. Often it is the area you avoid because you aren't good at it, which is exactly why it keeps holding you back.
cards.apply_it: Score yourself 1-10 in each of your key work areas. Choose the lowest score and plan one way to improve it this month.

quiz.question: Why does Tracy say you should work on your weakest key area?
options: Because a weakness in one key area can limit your overall results
Because weaknesses are easier to fix
quiz.explanation: One weak area can hold back performance in everything else.

cards.title: Find the three tasks that create most of your value
cards.body:
Tracy describes the law of three: among everything you do at work, roughly three tasks usually contribute most of your value. He tells of a client who listed all her work activities, picked out the three that mattered most, and agreed with her boss to focus on them and hand off much of the rest, with a big jump in results.

Knowing your three lets you guard them. If you spend most of your time on those few tasks, you produce more without working longer hours.
cards.apply_it: Write down everything you do in a typical week. Circle the three tasks that create the most value for your work.

quiz.question: What is Tracy's law of three?
options: Do three tasks per day, no more
A few core tasks, about three, account for most of your contribution
quiz.explanation: Focusing on the few highest-value tasks produces most of the results.

cards.title: Get everything ready before you begin a big task
cards.body:
Tracy notes that a common excuse for delay is not having what you need. His remedy is to prepare thoroughly: gather all the papers, information, tools and materials before you start, and set up a clean, comfortable workspace.

When everything is in place, starting becomes much easier, and you avoid breaking off halfway to hunt for something. Like a cook laying out ingredients before cooking, the preparation itself is a signal to your mind that it's time to work.
cards.apply_it: Before tomorrow's frog, gather everything you'll need for it and clear your workspace tonight.

quiz.question: Why does Tracy recommend preparing thoroughly before starting?
options: It is a good way to delay the task
Preparation is more important than the task
Having everything ready removes excuses and makes it easier to start and keep going
quiz.explanation: A ready workspace and materials remove friction and interruptions.

cards.title: Tackle a huge task by focusing only on the next step you can see
cards.body:
Tracy tells the story of a desert route across the Sahara that was marked with oil barrels placed at intervals within sight of each other. Travellers didn't need to see the whole route; they only had to reach the next barrel.

Big projects can feel the same: overwhelming as a whole, manageable one step at a time. You don't need every answer before you start. Go as far as you can see, and by the time you get there you will usually see far enough to keep going.
cards.apply_it: Take a project that feels overwhelming and write only the next single step. Do just that today.

quiz.question: What is the lesson of Tracy's oil barrel story?
options: You only need to see the next step to make progress on a big task
quiz.explanation: Moving from one visible marker to the next makes a huge task manageable.

cards.title: Keep upgrading your key skills so hard tasks feel doable
cards.body:
Tracy argues that people often procrastinate on tasks because they feel unsure they can do them well. One of the best cures is to keep learning: become better at the skills your key tasks require.

He recommends regular reading in your field, taking courses, and listening to educational audio during travel time. The more competent you become, the faster and more confidently you can start important work. Continuous learning turns frogs that once felt daunting into tasks you can handle.
cards.apply_it: Identify one skill whose weakness makes you avoid certain tasks. Spend 15 minutes learning about it today.

quiz.question: How does Tracy connect skill-building to procrastination?
options: Learning is a form of procrastination
Feeling unskilled makes us avoid tasks, so building skills helps us start
quiz.explanation: Greater competence reduces the doubt that causes delay.

cards.title: Put your energy where your special talents lie
cards.body:
Tracy encourages you to notice what you do especially well and enjoy most. These are often the areas where you can make your biggest contribution, and where your work feels easier and more satisfying.

He suggests asking what you're good at that others find hard, what has been most important to your success so far, and what people praise you for. Then try to arrange more of your work around those strengths, while still developing the skills your job requires.
cards.apply_it: Ask two colleagues or friends what they think you are best at. Look for ways to use that strength more this week.

quiz.question: What does Tracy advise about your special talents?
options: Ignore them and focus only on weaknesses
Identify what you do best and enjoy, and direct more of your work there
quiz.explanation: Your talents point to where you can contribute most effectively.

cards.title: Find the one bottleneck holding you back and fix that first
cards.body:
For any goal, Tracy says, there is usually one key constraint that limits how fast you reach it. It might be a missing skill, a slow process, a lack of customers, or a decision you've been avoiding.

Identifying that bottleneck and working on it can produce more progress than effort spread across everything else. He also claims that most constraints are inside us or our organisation, rather than outside. Asking 'What in me is holding me back?' is often more useful than blaming circumstances.
cards.apply_it: For one goal, ask: what single factor most limits my progress? Write one action to loosen it this week.

quiz.question: According to Tracy, where should you focus to speed up progress on a goal?
options: On the single key constraint that limits progress
quiz.explanation: Removing the main bottleneck has a bigger effect than spreading effort around.

cards.title: Set your own deadlines rather than waiting for pressure
cards.body:
Tracy observes that most people wait for someone else to push them. But nobody is coming to motivate you every day, so he suggests putting pressure on yourself: set your own deadlines, ideally earlier than the real ones, and act as if you had to finish today.

He proposes imagining you have been called away for a month and must finish your main task before you leave. That picture sharpens focus remarkably. Holding yourself to a high standard without being told to is a habit that sets people apart.
cards.apply_it: For your next big task, set a personal deadline a few days before the real one and write it in your calendar.

quiz.question: What does Tracy suggest instead of waiting for external pressure?
options: Wait for your boss to set deadlines
Set your own, earlier deadlines and hold yourself to them
quiz.explanation: Self-imposed deadlines create focus without relying on others to push you.

cards.title: Protect your energy with rest, exercise and regular breaks
cards.body:
Tracy points out that tiredness makes everything harder, including starting your frog. When you are worn out, you are more likely to put off important work and choose easy tasks instead.

He recommends looking after the basics: getting enough sleep, taking at least one full day off each week, eating well and exercising regularly. He also suggests noticing when your energy peaks during the day and saving that time for your most important work. Rest isn't a reward for productivity; it is part of what makes it possible.
cards.apply_it: Note the time of day you usually feel most alert. Schedule tomorrow's frog for that slot.

quiz.question: How does Tracy link energy and procrastination?
options: Being tired makes you more likely to avoid important tasks
Energy has nothing to do with it
quiz.explanation: Fatigue pushes you toward easy tasks; good rest and health support focused work.

cards.title: Coach yourself with optimistic, solution-focused thinking
cards.body:
Tracy encourages you to be your own cheerleader. Drawing on Martin Seligman's work on learned optimism, he describes habits of optimistic people: they look for something good in each situation, seek the lesson in setbacks, focus on solutions rather than blame, and keep thinking about their goals.

The way you talk to yourself shapes how you feel and act. Telling yourself you can handle a task, and asking 'What can I do now?' after a setback, makes it more likely that you'll start and keep going.
cards.apply_it: After your next setback, write one lesson from it and one next step, instead of dwelling on who's to blame.

quiz.question: Which habit does Tracy associate with optimistic people?
options: Looking for the lesson in every setback
quiz.explanation: Optimists look for lessons and solutions, which keeps them moving forward.

cards.title: Make technology your servant, not your master
cards.body:
Tracy warns that constant connection, with phones buzzing and email always open, can swallow the hours you need for important work. Reacting to every message keeps you busy without moving your priorities forward.

He suggests creating zones of silence: set periods, even whole days, when devices are off and you can think. He also argues that being reachable at every moment is rarely as essential as it feels. You decide when to check messages, rather than letting the devices decide for you.
cards.apply_it: Choose one daily period, even 60 minutes, when your phone is in another room and notifications are off. Use it for your frog.

quiz.question: What does Tracy mean by 'zones of silence'?
options: Set periods when you switch off devices to focus or rest
quiz.explanation: Planned device-free time protects focus from constant interruptions.

cards.title: Apply the 80/20 rule to your messages too
cards.body:
Tracy describes a client who was swamped by hundreds of emails a day. By recognising that only a small share needed his personal attention, and arranging for an assistant to sort and handle the rest, he freed up many hours each week.

You may not have an assistant, but the principle still applies: most messages don't need you right away, or at all. Use filters, unsubscribe from newsletters you don't read, batch replies at set times, and reply first to the few messages that matter most.
cards.apply_it: Unsubscribe from five mailing lists today, and set two fixed times to check messages tomorrow.

quiz.question: What lesson does Tracy draw from his client's email overload?
options: Only a few messages need your attention; filter or hand off the rest
Email is the most important task
quiz.explanation: Most messages are low-value; sorting them frees time for key work.

cards.title: Slice a big task into small pieces and do just one
cards.body:
Tracy calls this the salami-slice method. You wouldn't try to eat a whole salami at once; you cut it into thin slices. Likewise, break a big, intimidating task into small, specific steps and commit to finishing just one.

Completing one slice often gives you the urge to do the next. He talks about a drive towards closure: once you've finished a piece, you want to keep going. Breaking work down makes it less scary and gives you a steady sense of progress.
cards.apply_it: Write your frog at the top of a page and break it into five thin slices. Do the first one now.

quiz.question: What is the salami-slice method?
options: Eating a healthy lunch before working
Breaking a big task into thin, specific pieces and doing one at a time
quiz.explanation: Small slices make big tasks less intimidating and build momentum.

cards.title: Commit to just five or ten minutes on a task you're avoiding
cards.body:
Tracy's Swiss cheese method complements the salami slice. Instead of dividing the task by pieces, you divide it by time: commit to working on it for a short, fixed period, such as five or ten minutes, and then you're allowed to stop.

Like punching holes in a block of cheese, each short session chips away at the task. Often, once you've started, you'll want to keep going. Even if you don't, you've made real progress on something you might otherwise have avoided all day.
cards.apply_it: Set a 10-minute timer and work on the task you've been avoiding. When it rings, decide whether to continue.

quiz.question: How does the Swiss cheese method differ from the salami-slice method?
options: It divides the task by time rather than by pieces
It means skipping parts of the task
quiz.explanation: Swiss cheese means short, fixed time bursts; salami means small task pieces.

cards.title: Build a habit of acting quickly on important work
cards.body:
Tracy describes highly productive people as having a bias for action: rather than talking about a task, they get on with it. He suggests repeating a simple phrase like 'Do it now!' to push yourself past hesitation.

He also notes that getting started takes the most energy, while keeping going takes far less. A sense of urgency helps you overcome that starting hump and can lead into a state of deep focus where work flows. Over time, people who move quickly on important tasks also build a reputation for being dependable.
cards.apply_it: The next time you catch yourself hesitating on an important task, say 'Do it now' and start within 60 seconds.

quiz.question: According to Tracy, what takes the most energy when working on a task?
quiz.explanation: Starting is the hardest part; once moving, momentum makes continuing easier.

cards.title: Getting more done should give you more time for the people you love
cards.body:
Tracy reminds readers that productivity isn't the end goal. The reason to finish your most important work efficiently is to free up time for the things that make life meaningful, above all your relationships with family and friends.

He argues that relationships are among the biggest sources of happiness. If better time management only leads to more work, something has been missed. Focusing on what matters at work should leave you with more energy and hours for the people at home.
cards.apply_it: Use the time you save this week by eating your frog early to do one thing with someone you care about.

quiz.question: What does Tracy say is the deeper purpose of being productive?
options: To have a longer to-do list
To free time for what makes life meaningful, especially relationships
quiz.explanation: Productivity is a means to a fuller life, not an end in itself.

cards.title: Eating your frog is a skill you can learn through practice
cards.body:
Tracy insists that dealing with your most important task first is not a personality trait but a habit, and habits can be learned. He points to three qualities that help: a firm decision to build the habit, the discipline to practise it, and the determination to keep going until it sticks.

At first it takes effort; with repetition it becomes your natural way of working. He also claims that finishing important tasks brings a feeling of satisfaction that motivates you to repeat the pattern.
cards.apply_it: Commit to eating your frog first every workday for the next three weeks. Mark each day you do it on a calendar.

quiz.question: How does Tracy view the ability to do your most important task first?
options: As a habit anyone can learn through decision, discipline and repetition
quiz.explanation: It's a learnable habit that becomes natural with practice.

cards.title: Don't stare at your frog: start before the dread grows
cards.body:
One of Tracy's frog rules is that if you have to eat a live frog, it doesn't pay to sit and look at it for very long. The longer you think about an unpleasant task, the bigger and worse it seems.

Overthinking feeds anxiety and gives procrastination time to win. The fix is to take the first action quickly, before your mind builds a case against it. Once you are moving, the task usually turns out less painful than it looked from the outside.
cards.apply_it: Pick the task you've been worrying about longest. Take one small action on it in the next five minutes.

quiz.question: What does Tracy mean by not looking at the frog for too long?
options: Plan in detail before every task
Start quickly, because thinking too long makes a task seem worse
quiz.explanation: Delay and overthinking make a task loom larger; prompt action shrinks it.
